desc:
You start with a strip of target.length blank cells. In one turn you press the string stamp onto the strip at some position p such that the stamp lies completely inside the strip. The cells p .. p + stamp.length - 1 then show the letters of the stamp, replacing whatever was there before (blank or not).

You can press the stamp any number of times. Return true if the strip can be made to read exactly target, otherwise false.

stamp = "abc", target = "ababc"  -> true    (press at 0, then at 2)
stamp = "abc", target = "abcba"  -> false
stamp = "ab",  target = "abba"   -> false
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: The last press leaves an entire copy of the stamp visible in the target. Reason backwards from the end instead of forwards from a blank strip.

Reverse the process: find a window of the target that equals the stamp, erase it to wildcards, and repeat; a window may match when some of its cells are already wildcards, as long as at least one cell is still a real letter.

Keep for every window the set of cells that still disagree with the stamp. When a window's set becomes empty, erase its remaining letters, remove those cells from the neighbouring windows' sets, and push newly matching windows on a queue. The answer is true if every cell ends up erased.
editorial: Work backwards. The final press shows a complete copy of stamp in the target. Undo it: replace those cells by a wildcard ?, which matches any letter (those cells could have been overwritten by earlier presses in any way). The press before that one shows the stamp again, except that cells covered by later presses are now wildcards. So repeatedly undo a window that matches the stamp where wildcards are free, and that still contains at least one real letter (otherwise undoing it is pointless). The target is stampable exactly when everything can be turned into wildcards.

Undoing a window can only create more wildcards and never destroys a possible match elsewhere, so the order in which valid windows are undone does not matter: this is a closure computation, and it is correct to undo any available window greedily.

A naive rescan after each undo is too slow. Instead, for each of the at most n - m + 1 windows store its list of matching cells and the set of mismatching cells. When a window's mismatching set is empty, enqueue it. Processing a window turns each of its not-yet-erased matching cells into a wildcard; for every window containing such a cell, delete that cell from its mismatching set and enqueue the window if the set became empty. Every cell is erased once and touches at most m windows, so the total work is O(n · m).
